related.en: Well, now you can sit there

note:
A short «е̏» at the start of a phrase is very common in Serbian dialogue. Klajn's dictionary describes dozens of its meanings.

With it you can:
• call someone over - «Е̏, де̏во̄јко!»
• sigh - «Е, ко би рекао»
• admire - «Е, што је лепа!»
• agree - «Е̏, па до̀бро»
• sum things up - «Е, сад седи»
• start a new topic or warn someone - «Е, пази!»
title: The interjection «е» in everyday speech

note:
The English word Christmas is usually translated as Бо̀жић, but the traditions behind them are different.

In Serbia, Christmas falls on January 7 and there are no presents under the tree: the јелка is decorated for New Year.

On Christmas people:
• burn oak branches - ба̏дња̄к
• go to church
• say Христос се роди!
• wait for the положајник - the first guest of the year

New Year decorations in Serbian are новогодишњи украси.
title: Божић is not quite the same as Christmas

related.en: St Tryphon, patron saint of winegrowers

note:
St Valentine's Day in Serbia is Дан заљубљених. People feel differently about it:
• some consider it foreign to Orthodoxy
• others joke about it
• others are indifferent

Shops, however, are happy to run promotions.

For Orthodox believers this is the day of Све̑тӣ Три̏фӯн, the patron saint of winegrowers.

The greeting: Срећан Дан заљубљених!
title: February 14 in Serbia

note:
In everyday speech Serbs liberally pad their sentences with connecting words that are not in textbooks:
• ми̏слӣм - «I mean»
• ка̏о - «like»
• ово оно - «this and that»

There is no direct translation: they are just pause fillers. When you hear them, do not try to translate them literally, but catch the meaning around them.
title: Three Serbian filler words

related.en: a district of Belgrade named after the monument to Vuk

note:
Ву̑к is not only «wolf» but also a personal name: children were given it as a protective charm.

Vuk Stefanović Karadžić (1787-1864):
• reformed the writing system on the principle «write as you speak»
• created the modern alphabet
• collected folk songs and proverbs

A street and schools are named after him. In Belgrade there is a district called Вуков споменик, named after the monument to Vuk (спо̏менӣк means «monument»).
title: Вуков споменик is not a monument to a wolf

related.en: The switch needs to be replaced.
The boiler needs to be repaired.
I need to hang the mirror.
Water is leaking from the faucet.
The light bulb has burned out.

note:
What needs to be done:
• replace - Тре́ба заме́нити прекѝда̄ч
• repair - Тре́ба по̀правити ко̀тао
• hang - Треба да окачим огледало

How to explain what is broken:
• Цури вода из чесме
• Прегорела је сијалица
• Запушила се цев
• Не ра̏ди пе̑ћ

A request to the repairman: Молим вас да прикључите ...
title: Phrases for when something breaks at home

note:
Names of household items that are not in textbooks:
• подметач - trivet
• цѐдиљка - colander
• сецкалица за поврће - vegetable chopper
• оцеђивач за судове - dish rack
• ка̀луп за ле̑д - ice cube tray
• мерна чаша - measuring cup
• четка за ВЦ - toilet brush
• пр̀скалица - spray bottle

Ку̏ка is simply a hook, and кр̏па is a rag and also a kitchen towel.
title: Small things for the kitchen and home

related.en: cream slice (custard between layers of puff pastry)
meringue cream on a sponge base
Jaffa Cakes (sponge cookies with orange jelly and chocolate)

note:
Pastry-shop classics:
• кре̏мпита - a thick layer of cream between layers of puff pastry
• шампита - fluffy white meringue cream on a sponge base
• принцес крофна - a cream puff

Turkish cuisine left behind туфа̀хија (apples in syrup with walnuts), када́иф, орашница and су̏тлија̄ш.

From store-bought sweets: јафа кејк, бананица, наполитанке.

Тулумбе are little fingers of dough soaked in syrup.
title: Serbian desserts

note:
Бо̑л is masculine in Serbian, so adjectives with it are masculine too.

How to describe pain:
• by strength: сла̏б, у̀мерен, ја̑к, непо̀дношљив
• by duration: про́лазан, у̏по̄ран, хро̀ничан, и̏знена̄дан
• by character: ту̑п, о̏штар, пулси́рајӯћи, уба́дајӯћи, пѐкӯћи

The pain comes in attacks: бол се јавља у нападима.

Unpleasant sensations in general - те̏гобе, cramps - гр̀чеви, pins and needles - трнци.
title: How to describe pain to a doctor

related.sr: Тра̏жим ста̑н, Но̏ви Бео̀град, до 400 е̏вра, непу̀шачи, без ку̏ћних љу̀бӣма̄ца̄
related.en: Looking for an apartment, New Belgrade, up to 400 euros, non-smokers, no pets

note:
Three things give away a foreigner on Serbian social media:
• Serbs use real emoji rather than typed smileys
• they love sending стикере in reply to До̀бро ју̏тро!
• housing ads are short and to the point, without family photos or self-introductions

An example: Тражим стан, Нови Београд, до 400 евра, непушачи, без кућних љубимаца
title: How Serbs communicate on social media

note:
The basics:
• сло̏во - letter, ре̑ч - word
• гла̑с - sound
• са̏могласнӣк, су̀гласнӣк - vowel, consonant
• на́гласак - accent, а̀кценат - stress

Parts of speech: и̏меница, за̑меница, при́дев, гла̏гол, при́лог, пре́длог, ве̑знӣк, ре̏чца, у̏звӣк.

Categories: ро̑д, бро̑ј (једнѝна, множѝна), па́деж.

There are seven cases, the last of them the vocative, and their names are Latin-based: но̏минатӣв, ге̏нитӣв, да́тӣв, а̏кузатӣв, и̏нструмента̄л, ло̏катӣв, во̏катӣв.
title: Grammatical terms in Serbian

note:
In fast speech Serbs shorten words:
• ишао - ишо
• ви̑део - видо
• да урадим - дурадим

That is how people talk, but not how they write: in writing the full forms remain.

Sometimes Serbs jokingly write down the colloquial pronunciation, and such spelling is hard to decipher.
title: How people speak, as opposed to how they write

note:
In the 19th century the New Testament was translated into the vernacular by Vuk Karadžić and the Old Testament by Đura Daničić. This was an important step for the Serbian literary language.

Many biblical expressions are still alive in the language, although they contain a lot of archaic forms:
• the ending -ога: ближњега свога
• the participle вапијући
• the verb иштите
title: The first Bible translations into the vernacular

related.sr: Ча̏к Но̏рис мо̀же да де̏ли и ну̏лом
related.en: Chuck Norris can even divide by zero

related.sr: Ка̏д Ча̏к Но̏рис се̏че лу̏к, не пла̑че о̑н, не̏го лу̏к
related.en: When Chuck Norris cuts an onion, it is not him who cries but the onion

note:
In Serbia, «Chuck Norris facts» have become part of the folklore of jokes (ви̏ц), next to the heroes Перица, Мујо and Хасо.

They are short exaggerations about an all-powerful hero:
• Чак Норис може да дели и нулом
• Кад Чак Норис сече лук, не плаче он, него лук
title: Chuck Norris in Serbian humor

note:
In colloquial Serbian, things are often named after the people they are associated with:
• титовка - a partisan cap with a star
• ленинка - a peaked cap
• фа̀нто̄мка - a balaclava
• исусовке - strappy sandals
• тарзанка - a hairstyle with short sides
• ленонке - round glasses
• терминаторке - high sneakers
• спенсерице - light lace-up boots

These names are informal.
title: Things named after people

note:
Many cities sound different from their English names:
• Мѝнхен, Па̀рӣз, Марсеј, Мила̑но
• На́пуљ, Фиренца, Бе̑ч
• Брѝсел, Бу̏курешт, Даблин

Gender: Бу̀димпешта is feminine, while Пра̏г, Казањ and Перм are masculine: у Казању, из Казања, до Перма.
title: City names in Serbian

related.en: Come here, I won't do anything to you

related.sr: Оста̀ви те ко̀лаче, то̑ је за го̏сте
related.en: Leave those cakes alone, they are for the guests
Can Milica come out to play?

related.sr: Нарѐзаћу ти на ЦД омѝљене пе̏сме
related.en: I'll burn your favorite songs onto a CD for you
Call me, I don't have enough credit

note:
Serbs now in their forties remember the 90s through phrases:
• Дођи, нећу ти ништа - the parental «threat»
• Остави те колаче, то је за госте - the best is kept for guests
• Може ли Милица напоље? - asking parents to let a child out to play
• Нарезаћу ти на ЦД омиљене песме
• Назови ме, немам довољно кредита

These are recognizable marks of the time: childhood on the street, discs, cassettes and prepaid phones.
title: Phrases from a Serbian childhood in the 90s

note:
The colloquial ћа̑о (both «hi» and «bye») traveled this way:
1. Medieval Latin sclavus - «Slav», later «slave».
2. Venetian s-ciavo - «I am your servant».
3. Italian ciao.
4. Serbian ћа̑о.

The formula «I am your servant» gradually turned into a greeting. The native Slavic counterpart is здра̏во.
title: Where «ћао» comes from

note:
The interjections ја̏о and јој are not limited to «oh no». Depending on intonation and context they express:
• annoyance - Јао, заборавила сам телефон!
• delight - Ја̏о, што̏ је ле̑по!, Јој, преслатко!

Only ја̏о takes the dative: Ја̏о мѐнӣ!, Јао онима који...
title: Јао and јој: not only negative

related.en: exam at the end of elementary school

note:
The school system in Serbia:
1. вр̀тић - kindergarten.
2. The zero grade and основна школа (grades 1-8).
3. Гѝмна̄зија or стручна школа.

The school year is divided into two полугодишта, with a зи̑мскӣ ра́спуст and a летњи распуст.

At the end of elementary and secondary school students take the малу матуру and the матуру.

The class monitor is the председник одељења.
title: The school system in Serbia

note:
What foreigners find hard to pronounce:
• long words: државља́нство, посластѝчарница
• the syllabic «Р» among other consonants: твр̀ђава, стр̏шље̄н, нерђајући челик, чвр̏шћӣ
• the soft «Љ», a single sound like «lli» in «million»: љу̀ља̄шка
• unstressed «О», which stays a clear «О» and is not reduced: по̀сао, по̀родица
title: What foreigners find hard to pronounce

skip: comparison of Serbian and Russian pronunciation only

note:
The 3rd person plural pronoun has three forms, by gender:
• о̀ни - masculine
• оне - feminine
• она - neuter

The endings match the plural of nouns of the same gender:
• при̏јатељи - они - добри
• девојке - оне - лепе
• дѐца - она - вредна

Де́те is neuter, so дѐца is «она». A mixed group of men and women is «они».
title: Three «they»: они, оне, она

note:
Family is important in Balkan culture, so there are many words for relatives.
• father's brother - стри̑ц
• mother's brother - у̏ја̄к
• an aunt, on either side - те̏тка

The uncles' wives have their own names too: стри̑на, у̏јна.

A grandmother may affectionately call a girl си̑не as well.
title: Relatives: uncles and aunts

note:
Almost every profession has a separate word for a man and for a woman: лѐка̄р - лѐкарка.

These double forms developed in the language and a few years ago were made official in the norm. So lists of professions have twice as many words.
title: Professions: masculine and feminine forms

note:
A nationality has separate words for a man, a woman, the plural and the language: Ср̏бин, Ср̏пкиња, Срби, ср̏пскӣ.

The name of the language is written with a small letter, the other forms with a capital (unlike in English).

To answer the question «where?» you need the locative: Жи́вӣм у Нѐмачко̄ј.
title: Nationalities: four words

skip: comparison of Serbian and Russian sounds only

note:
In colloquial Serbian, syllables are sometimes swapped as a joke: тра̀фика becomes фикатра.

In dialects the «х» is also often lost:
• ладно instead of хла́дно
• леб instead of хле̏б
• оћеш instead of хоћеш

So be ready for such forms.
title: Syllable games and dropping «х» in colloquial speech

related.en: How fast does a little peach run?

note:
In winter in Serbia people take out пичигузе - small plastic sleds with a handle, which children and adults ride down hills.

By a joking etymology, the word is made of пичити (to rush, to dash) and гуз (backside): «a rushing backside».

There is also a pun: Колико брзо трчи мала бресква? - Peachy. The English «peachy» sounds like «пичи».
title: Пичигуз - the «bum sled»

note:
Пла̑в means both «blue» and «blond»: пла̑ва ко̀са is light hair, blond, and the sky and the sea are also «плаво».

In Old Slavic «плав» described what is light, pale or golden. For blue there used to be the words мо̏дар and си̑њӣ: модро море.

The meaning depends on the context.
title: Плава коса is not blue hair

note:
The standard Serbian accent combines pitch and stress: a syllable stands out not only by force but also by tone.

It can be long or short, rising or falling - four types in all: ру́ка, жѐна, ма̑јка, бра̏т.

Tone and length can tell words apart: гра̑д «city» and гра̑д «hail».

In everyday speech many people speak more simply, with a single stress accent, and are understood. Variants like ауто́бус are acceptable.
title: The four Serbian accents

note:
Serbia was part of the Ottoman Empire for several centuries, and thousands of Turkish words entered the language. Half of them are obsolete, but about three thousand are alive in daily life:
• ја̀стук, ко̀мшија, ба́шта
• ра̀кија, сѝрће, ка̀фа
• шѐћер, бу̀рек

Often a «Slavic» variant exists alongside, but the Turkism sounds more natural.
title: Turkisms in everyday speech

note:
In Serbian, the names of countries and their inhabitants are written with a capital letter, but the language is not (unlike in English).

For each country there is a masculine and a feminine form for the inhabitant, and an adjective:
• Ср̀бија - Ср̏бин - Ср̏пкиња - ср̏пскӣ
• Нѐмачка̄ - Не́мац - Нѐмица - нѐмачкӣ
• Ки́на - Кѝне̄з - Кѝне̄скиња - кѝне̄скӣ
• Ѐнгле̄ска̄ - Ѐнгле̄з - Ѐнглескиња - ѐнгле̄скӣ
title: Countries, peoples and languages: the capital letter

note:
Serbs switch from ви̑ to ти quickly: even a shop cashier may say ћа̑о.

Formally, one says господине / госпођо / госпођице + surname in the vocative: господине Јовановићу. It is also fine without a surname.

Мо̀мак and дѐво̄јка are not used as forms of address.
title: How to address people: ти or ви

related.en: a film without a happy ending

note:
Figurative expressions about Russia in colloquial speech:
• руска салата - Russian salad (Olivier)
• руска зима - very severe cold
• ру̏скӣ фи̏лм - a film without a happy ending, where the hero loses everything

These are stereotypes: it is useful to know them, but do not take them for neutral words.
title: «Russian» expressions among Serbs

related.en: a metal baking lid, covered with embers
a dish baked under a сач

note:
Јело испод сача is a dish that is slowly cooked under a сач: a metal lid covered with hot coals.

Most often it is meat with vegetables, for example тѐлетина or ја̀гњетина. The dish is considered home cooking and festive food.
title: Јело испод сача

related.en: first floor (second floor by American count)

note:
An address usually includes:
• the street and the house number
• у̀лаз (entrance)
• спра̏т (floor)
• ста̑н (apartment)
• по̏штанскӣ бро̑ј (postal code) and the city

The ground floor is при́зе̄мље: it does not count as a спра̏т (it is the zero one). So пр̀вӣ спра̏т is already the second floor by American count.

The intercom is и̏нтерфон, its code is ши̏фра.
title: Addresses and floors in Serbia

note:
On a walk with a dog you hear:
• дођи - come
• седи - sit
• ста̏ни - stop
• чекај - wait
• пу̑стӣ - drop it
• ти̏хо - quiet
• ха̀јде - let's go

For praise people say је л тако or бра̏во.

These are everyday words, and they work in ordinary speech too.
title: Commands for a dog

related.en: bogeywoman, a forest witch with a horn

note:
Бабаро́га is a character of Serbian ба̑јкӣ, related to the Russian Baba Yaga: an old forest вѐштица with a horn on her forehead, who lives in dark caves.

She is used to scare children, and by one version she comes to sleeping children at night.

The word ба̏ба here means «old woman».
title: Бабарога

note:
In messages Serbs write in the Latin alphabet and abbreviate words:
• vrv - ве̏рова̄тно
• msm - ми̏слӣм
• nmg - не мо̀гу
• nzm - не зна̑м

The abbreviations are clear if you know the full form. Cyrillic is rarely seen in such messages.
title: Abbreviations in text messages

note:
Names for shopping:
• чоколадно млеко - chocolate
• млеко у праху - powdered
• кондензовано млеко - condensed
• биљно млеко - plant-based
• млеко без лактозе - lactose-free

Plant-based kinds are named after their base: сојино, бадемово, пиринчано, кокосово.

Baby formula is фо̑рмула за бебе́.
title: Kinds of milk in the store

note:
Fingers of the hand:
• па̏лац - thumb
• ка̀жипрст - index finger
• сре̏дњӣ пр̏ст - middle finger
• домали прст - ring finger
• ма̏лӣ пр̏ст - little finger

Пр̏ст means both a finger and a toe: ножни прст.

The nail is но̏кат.
title: Names of the fingers

note:
Ки̏шобра̄н consists of ки̏ша (rain) and бра́нити (to defend): «protection from rain».

The same pattern gives су̏нцобра̄н - a sunshade, a beach umbrella.

Note the connecting «о».
title: An umbrella against rain and against sun

skip: only about the Russian construction «мы с Владимиром»

note:
Titles of books and films often sound different in Serbian:
• «Gone with the Wind» - Прохујало с вихором
• «Crime and Punishment» - Зло̀чин и ка̏зна
• «The Lord of the Rings» - Госпо̀да̄р прстено́ва̄
• «Poverty Is No Vice» - Сирома́штво нѝје по̀рок

A good way to remember new words.
title: Titles of books and films

note:
Ма̀те̄рњӣ јѐзик - native language.

Names of languages are written with a small letter (unlike in English) and end in -ски:
• ру̏скӣ, у̀крајӣнскӣ, белоруски, јѐрме̄нскӣ
• ѐнгле̄скӣ, нѐмачкӣ, фра̀нцӯскӣ, италѝја̄нскӣ
• грузијски, албански, фи̑нскӣ, пољски
• ту̀рскӣ, гр̏чкӣ, сло̀веначкӣ, макѐдо̄нскӣ
title: Native language and names of languages

skip: false friend with Russian ягодицы only

note:
Fairy tales in Serbian often have different titles from English:
• «Sleeping Beauty» - Успавана лепотица
• «Little Red Riding Hood» - Црвенкапа
• «Tom Thumb» - Тома Палчић
• «Cinderella» - Пепѐљуга

This helps to remember the words лепо̀тица and успавана.
title: Fairy tales in Serbian

related.en: meat roasted on a spit (suckling pig, lamb)
a restaurant serving roast meat; a spit oven

note:
Пѐче̄ње is meat roasted on a spit, usually a suckling pig or a lamb.

A cookie or biscuit is ке̏кс.

A place that roasts meat is called a печѐњара, and so is the spit oven itself.
title: Печење: roast meat

note:
Loved ones are affectionately called: ср̏це, ду́ша, ме̑д, зве́зда, зла̑то, су̑нце, ма́ца, бе́ба, мала.

Such words are used both in direct address and in conversation.
title: Terms of endearment

note:
Beer can be та̑мно (dark), све̏тло (light) or точено (draft).

Wine: бело (white), црно (red), ро̀зе ви́но, домаће (homemade).

Spirits: ра̀кија, во̑тка, ви̏ски, ко̏ња̄к, вѐрмут.
title: Drinks: beer and wine

skip: about the Russian name Люда only

note:
On November 11 Serbia marks Armistice Day of the First World War. It is a не̏радни да̑н.

The symbol of the day is the flower Наталијина рамонда, which «resurrects» after a drought.

Vocabulary for the day: се̏ћа̄ње, јунаци.
title: Armistice Day: the ramonda

note:
Serbs fill pauses with words:
• зна̏чи - «so»
• па - «well»
• о̀ва̄ј - «uh», «what's-it-called»
• ми̏слӣм - «I mean»
• бу̏ква̄лно - often just for emphasis

They occur in almost every conversation.
title: Filler words

note:
In Serbia blood types are marked with the international system: O, A, B, AB and the Rh factor - позитивна or негативна.

For example: «O позитивна» is O positive, «AB негативна» is AB negative.
title: Blood type

related.en: roast suckling pig on a spit

note:
On a New Year's table in Serbia you usually find:
• пѐче̄ње - roast suckling pig
• руска салата
• а̀јва̄р
• пита са сиром
• ку̏лен, ка̀јмак
• бакла̀ва
• ва̀нилице
• сла̀тко̄ од шљи̏ва
• са̀рма
title: The New Year table

related.en: oak branch that is burned in the evening

note:
Бадњи дан (January 6) is Christmas Eve. People bring a ба̏дња̄к into the house - an oak branch that is burned in the evening.

The table is meatless: па̀сӯљ, ри̏ба, ораси.

For Бо̀жић people bake a чесница with a coin in it.

On the three Sundays before Christmas family members are «tied up»:
• Детињци - children
• Материце - mothers
• О̀ци - fathers

The ransom is sweets and presents.
title: Christmas customs

note:
Некрштени дани is the period from Christmas to Богојављење (January 19).

By tradition, Christ is not yet baptized, the border between the worlds is thin, and evil spirits roam. In the past people did not leave the house at night, protected children and pregnant women, and postponed important matters.

They protected themselves from evil forces with garlic (бе̑лӣ лу̏к), the fire of the hearth and prayer. Today this is more a part of folklore.
